maintopic: MESSAGE FROM THE GOVERNOR GENERAL-MAIN ESTIMATES.

speechtext:
Rt. Hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister) delivered a message from the Governor General.

Grey.
Government' House,
Ottawa, January 18, 1905.
The Governor General transmits to the House of Commons estimates of sums required for the service of the Dominion for the year ending June 30, 1906, and in accordance with the provisions of the B. N. A., 1867, the Governor General recommends these estimates to the House of Commons.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
speechtext:
PATERSON (Minister of Customs) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.
Hon., GEO. JE. FOSTER. Before the House goes into Committee of Supply, there are two points upon which I would like to have information, if convenient to the ministers. I noticed in newspapers of a



late date a statement that the proposed steamship communication, with mutual subsidies I suppose, between Canada and Mexico, had run up against some difficulty. The minister who has had that matter in charge is in his place, and I would like to know how it stands at present.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
speechtext: Last spring the Mexican government agreed with the Canadian government to grant a subsidy of $50,000 in gold towards establishing two lines of steamers between Canada and Mexico, one on the Pacific ocean and the other on the Atlantic. The Canadian government, in pursuance of that understanding, asked and obtained a vote from this parliament of $50,000 last session, and the Mexican government did the same. I understand that the Department of Trade and Commerce invited tenders for both services, and received tenders ; but the tenders were quite in excess of the total sum of $100,000 gold voted by the two governments.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
speechtext: Were they monthly services ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
speechtext:
Yes, monthly sailings. Negotiations I think, were entered into by the tenderers for the Pacific servicespeaking from memory, I think the names were Weir & Co., of Glasgow-with a view of making, some modifications in the specifications and details. A representative of that company, after consulting with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, left him, expressing his intention of proceeding to Mexico and presenting some request to the Mexican government. I am not aware if he has yet had this interview with the Mexican government. But when I was in Mexico in the month of December last, the Mexican government informed me that they were much disappointed at the amount of money demanded for the service on the Pacific ; and without explaining to me what they had definitely in view, they did suggest that the proposition for completing that contract should stand over for a short time until Sir Weetman Pearson, a very eminent engineer, a man who is carrying on very large works in Mexico for the government, should reach Mexico, and then the government of that country would discuss the subject with him with a view to proceeding with the matter. They have no desire to withdraw from it, but they seein to think that perhaps they could make some arrangements through him that would be helpful to the scheme in view. But they expressed a willingness to grant at their approaching Congress another subsidy of $50,000 in gold, if we would do the same, for the establishment of a line on the Atlantic. That would mean that the Mexican government would contribute $100,000 in gold and we would contribute $100,000 in gold, by which we would get at least a Mr. FOSTER.
monthly sailing on the Atlantic and on the Pacific. Therefore, as X understand it, there is nothing now in the way of our completing an arrangement for the Atlantic if we can get it within the subsidy ; and the Mexican goveriynent think they will be able to arrange for the completion of a similar service on the Pacific. I think we may hopefully regard the prospects and that we may iiave both services in operation within a reasonable time.

Under what authority is that arbitration proceeding, and will the results, in so far as the evidence is concerned, toe presented to the House when the arbitration is finished ? Is it by commission or by virtue of the agreements themselves between the two parties ?

It is sub judice at the present time.

This is an arbitration in respect of differences that have arisen between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the government under diverse contracts entered into at different times. One of them was

entered into in 1879 in connection with the purchase of the line of railway from RiviSre du Loup to Point L&vis, and another has arisen out of the purchase of the extension of the line from Levis to St. Hyacinthe. There has been no action entered by the Crown, but the Crown has had claims against the Grand Trunk Railway arising out of what they claim to be the non-fulfilment by the company of these contracts. speechtext: I will give the hon. gentlenmni (Mr. Foster)1 the explanation that the Auditor General has given me. We need to have an additional officer in connection with the auditing of those accounts. There is also provision for eleven third-class clerks, who are not, however, to be new employees, they are now temporary, and are not to have their pay increased. Those eleven are in the service now, but he thinks it would be more desirable to place them upon the permanent list.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: PURCHASE OF THE CANADA ATLANTIC RAILWAY.

Eight first-class clerks, two at $1,900, one at $1,700, one at $1,600, four at $1,550, $13,300.

Messrs. Saunders, Bliss, Watson, Bristol, Gleeson and Frost.

subtopic: PURCHASE OF THE CANADA ATLANTIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Here is a large increase in high class clerks.

speechtext: These are the second-class clerks. This is to provide for statutory increases to Messrs. Ackers, Campbell, Grafton, Roper and Rorke, $50 each. Goodspeed and Telford, were estimated in 1904-5 at $1,250 in error, as their salaries were only $1,200, so that the statutory increases for 1905-6 are provided by leaving the estimates for their salaries the same as they were in 1904-5. Then I am making provision for four additional second-class clerks, three at $1,200 and one at $1,250, making an increase of $4,850.

A second-class clerkship shall only be created by Order in Council passed on the report of the deputy head, concurred in by the head of the department, setting forth the reasons for creating the office, and after the salary has been voted by parliament.

speechtext: That is right, there is no doubt ; but that is not the point that my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) was examining. I may say in a general way that owing to the provisions of what is known familiarly as the Dumping Clause Act, and the regulations that we have had to make, and the steps we have had to take, in order to ensure compliance with the law, additions to the staff have been necessitated. We feel sure that we cannot get along with less than this number if the work is to be done efficiently, as no doubt it is desired to be done. Therefore, we propose to transfer, if the committee sanctions this expenditure that we are asking for, from the outside staff of the Board of Customs four ifficers. The Board of Customs is connected with and is paid for out of the outside vote, the reason being because the work which is done here now in Ottawa in the central office is really outside work that used to be done at the ports in days gone by. But when it was thought desirable to get out a statement of exports and imports and of the general trade and commerce of the country once a month, and it could only be accomplished by bringing those who were engaged in the work of the outside ports to Ottawa and having all the information furnished here, it was decided to make that change. Therefore, there are men in the office who are well qualified for the inside service for the checking of invoices and so on, and that work will now be done more thoroughly than heretofore, and it has been thought desirable to bring some of the gentlemen who have had experience in dealing with these matters from the outside to the inside sex-vice.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: PURCHASE OF THE CANADA ATLANTIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
No. It has always been the law of Canada since confederation, that the duties should be levied upon the value of the articles in the country of export at the time of export. It is our duty' to see that that is done. An improvement, as I consider it, was made a few years ago. The old system was that a person buying goods from a foreign country and importing them had to have affixed to the invoice a certificate made by the party from whom he purchased the goods, certifying that the price given was cori'ect. The seller might sell the goods at from ten to twenty per cent below the current market price to the Canadian customer, and that being a bona fide transaction between himself and the buyer he could quite honestly attach the certificate because it was correct as to the transaction between the two individuals, and we of course never questioned the right of a man to sell his goods at any price he chose, but the law imposes on the department the duty of saying that the duty must be levied upon the value of the goods as sold in the counti'y of expoi't. Thex-efore that certificate was changed and it was required that the exporter should cei'tify that the prices mentioned were the prices at which the goods were sold in the country of export, and if there was any variation in that regard it was noted in the

margin. That helped us a good deal to secure the duties that were required under the law better than they had been secured before that time. But, when parliament adopted as additional taxation 50 per cent of the amount of cutting if you allow that expression, it became even more important than before that we should secure all information that would not harass trade, but would enable us to carry out the law as it was intended. We have therefore required under the new regulations more than one invoice. Hitherto two copies of the invoice came to this country. The merchant kept one himself and the law required that one should be furnished the customs and should be left at the port of entry. The entry was all that reached the department here. The entry would be scrutinized by the check department, and if they thought from anything in the descriptions that the local officer had not been able to ascertain the correct value for duty, the port had to be written to to forward the invoice, which then had to be examined here by-the check clerk, and if it was found that an error had been made the importer vyoulci be written to.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: PURCHASE OF THE CANADA ATLANTIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: An error in what way ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: PURCHASE OF THE CANADA ATLANTIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: For instance if the port officer had allowed articles to pass at a certain value which was an honest value as between buyer and seller but was not the value required by law on which the duty should be paid. When an error of this kind was discovered, a call would be made upon the importer who had made the entry in good faith to amend the entry and pay the difference. That entailed time and a good deal of irritation on the part of merchants because when an error occurred at a distant point, a good deal of time was lost in correspondence and by the time the demand was made for the additional duty, the merchant might have marked the goods and sold them, allowing for duty at the lower rate. We therefore thought that it was desirable to ask for two copies of the. invoice. This of course caused a little irritation at the time as all customs changes do, but I myself thought that this change was required long ago. One copy of the invoice is kept at the port of entry as before, but the other copy comes to the central office, so that day by day we have the entries to scrutinize, whereas previously we had to write to the port for each individual entry when required. If any failure to appreciate the requirements of the law on the part of the local collector is discovered we can notify him quickly, and in this way we have done away with a great deal of the irritation that was caused by asking a man to amend an entry perhaps two weejts after it was made. In order to do this we have required additional help and the staff has been increased in that way. I think that parliament will see that the trade and commerce of the country and the revenue warrant us in asking this additional help.

subtopic: PURCHASE OF THE CANADA ATLANTIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
That is the point I wish to make, that you have filled their places. Suppose that goods are brought in say at Shelburne, in Nova Scotia. One invoice is displayed there, the local officer passes upon it and collects the duty. Then a duplicate of the invoice and the entry is sent to Ottawa. All this supposes two things, that the local man in Shelburne shall have a knowledge of the current sale prices, say in Austria or Birmingham, or wherever the goods are bought. The difficulty seems to be how he is to know whether the prices that are on the invoice are simply the dealing prices between the seller and the buyer or the current prices at which the goods are sold in the market where they are bought. Does the local man, in Shelburne, or Guysboro', or anywhere else in this country, have a sufficient knowledge to adjudicate in a matter of that kind ? If so, how does he get it ?
I suppose that here in Ottawa you are better armed and equipped ; the men here do know. Have they an ubiquitous intuition as to the current prices of the goods in the country from which they are imported ? There must be a great deal of haphazard in the matter, and delay and dissatisfaction. After all, does not the hon. gentleman find a great deal of difficulty of getting at these current prices, and what machinery has he for doing it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: PURCHASE OF THE CANADA ATLANTIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
There is difficulty, of course, even in our larger offices, where our regular appraisers are very well posted. The way the matter is attended tio is this : One of our new regulations, winich I omitted to mention before, is the one that was complained of a little in Great Britain. English merchants, who are accustomed to free trade and who are not hampered with any customs regulations, did not seem to see the necessity of it. Under the new system, if there is any change in the price, we not only require the exporter to note it on the margin of the certificate, but we have double columns in which we require him to

enter the price at which the goods are sold in the country of export and the price at which they are sold to the Canadian importer. They said: What is the use of filling out the second column when the prices are the same ? Our reason for that is this : Hitherto they had to make a declaration that there was no change in the prices. That was apt sometimes1 to be performed in a perfunctory manner by a careless house, which would put its stamp on the declaration ; but greater care Is likely to be exercised when the price of each item has to be entered in two columns, and the exporter has to make a declaration that these entries are true and correct. If he puts down prices that are not correct, he is, of course, liable to all the penalties under the customs law, which are very severe. So that all the collectors now have invoices with these double columns, in which are entered opposite each item the price at which the goods are sold in the country of export, and the price at which they are sold to the Canadian consumer. Where there is a difference between the two, the collector adds the difference to the duty, but not exceeding fifty per cent of the duty on the article. i do not think It is a hardship. 1 think the English merchants who expressed some vexation with it, have realized that our regulations must be general in their nature, and that exceptions cannot be made in favour of one country over another. I think the department has succeeded in establishing pretty safe checks, which, when the system is understood and in practice for a time, will be found not to be harassing at all, either to exporter or importer. The collector relies necessarily on the invoice being bona fide in the first place. Our staff, I may say, has been increased, for we have thought it necessary to establish, in the country to the south of us, special agents, whose duty it is to ascertain and to put forward to the department here, the values of all leading articles. We have these agents at New York, Chicago, Boston, Seattle and Cleveland. These cities are their headquarters, but they cover the whole country among them. What is called the cutting of prices is more in vogue on the other side of the line than in England. The information iin regard to leading lines is coming to us daily, and is sent by circular to the different local officers. This, in a general way, -is, I think, the information the bon. gentleman wants. That we are deceived sometimes is possible; it is impossible that it can be otherwise; but we have taken all the precautions that we thought necessary. If any one passes a wrong entry, either designedly or in error, the matter does not end with the passing of the entry. There is no limit to the time that we can follow the importers for the duty itself; but' we can follow them for three years for the penalties, which in the extreme amount to the forfeiture of the
goods. Therefore, people will be careful, at any rate, houses with a reputation and standing, both importers and exporters, to make proper entries.

If he wants to give a Canadian a good bargain, you prevent him. You will not let him sell to a Canadian at a cent less than to one of his own fellow-Englisbmen or to a foreigner. speechtext: There has been no conversion because under our policy, if you can suppose an English merchant selling to a Canadian at. less than he does to others, we simply charge an extra tariff and give a portion of the benefit to the treasury. But if the hon. gentleman had his way, he would double the duty against the Englishman and make it impossible for him to sell to ns at all. WTe only collect an extra duty when the English merchants are able to sell at a lower rate. The duty of 30 per cent might become a duty of 35 per cent, but the hon. gentleman would make it fifty per cent. With us when the prices are so cheap, instead of the consumer getting the whole benefit, the treasury gets a portion and we are able to reduce taxation in another direction.

I wish to call the attention of the minister again to the statute with reference to this item. The minister knows it is not a new question. We have had it up during several sessions, and I have not yet been able to convince the hon. gentleman or any of his colleagues that

they ought to comply with the statute regarding these increases. I presume that the Civil Service Act was passed with some definite object. The clear intent of the statute was to put the responsibility for these increases upon, not tlie minister, but the permanent heads of the departments, as being the ones who know to what extent sucli increases are necessary. The permanent head of the department is required to make a report, that report has to be approved by the minister himself, then parliament votes the money ; and after all that is done, an Order in Council is passed creating the new clerkship. If you take section 15 of the Act, you cannot have any doubt as to the intention of parliament. Section 15 relates to the chief clerkships, and all the other sections follow in the same words, though not divided in the same way. That section provides that a new clerkship in any department shall only be created by Order in Council, to be passed after certain procedure has been followed. Three things must first be done. The deputy head must first report that such an officer is necessary for the proper performance of the public business in the department interested and must state the reasons on which he has arrived at 11'at conclusion. That surely does not mean that the deputy or permanent head of the departmeut must simply look at the item and not express any dissent. He Is expected to make a formal report to the minister giving the reasons for the increase. That being done, the minister must approve of his report or it can go no further. Having given his approval, the money must be voted by parliament, but what does the minister do ? He reverses all that. He first comes to parliament and asks for a vote. But how ridiculous would it not be for parliament to vote the money and then have the permanent head refuse to take the responsibility of recommending .that the extra clerks are essential to the working of the department. The procedure required by the Act is however reversed, and we are told that because the deputy minister has seen the item and has not objected to it, that is a sufficient compliance with the Act. Surely the minister will not pretend that that is a compliance with the statute. I would like the Minister of Justice to say whether he thinks it is? Here we have a $12,000 increase in these two items in the Customs Department, and we are entitled to ask the Minister of Justice whether the Minister of Customs has complied with the law ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.

speechtext:
This question was up for consideration several times during the previous session, being raised by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker). At the time, it appeared to me that the statute was perfectly clear? As I understand it, in the first place, the minister comes to parliament for a money vote to enable him to create a clerkship, of whatever class it may Mr. BARKER.
be. If parliament approves the suggestion of the minister and supplies the money, it is upon the condition that the deputy head-the permanent head, as my hon. friend calls him-shall make his report, and that report, confirmed by Council will be the justification for the minister to apply the money voted by parliament. This, it seems to me, is the clear meaning of the section. But. at the time the point was raised, in view of the argument put forward by my hon. friend, I thought it well to consult the deputy Minister of Justice, who has been in charge of the department for many years- ever since 1890 or 1891, I think. And he told me that this was the practise that had been invariably followed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT.
speechtext:
Before the motion is put,
I desire to call attention to the fact, that we have not received the public accounts, nor have we the Auditor General's Report. Probably the First Minister will be able to tell us when the Auditor General's Report will be down. We have gone on with the Civil Service Estimates, but we cannot go much further without the public accounts-

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT.
speechtext: The Public Accounts have been distributed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT.
speechtext: I think not. A copy was laid on the table, but members of the House have mot received copies. And, with reference to the Auditor General's Report, the First Minister will see that we cannot go much further with the estimates until we have received that report.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT.
speechtext: I can hold out little hope of an early distribution of the Auditor General's Report. The last account I had of it was two or three days ago. There were then in the hands of the Auditor General proofs for about ICO pages ; but there are about 300 pages of manuscript yet to come.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT.
speechtext: We are paying for eleven more clerks which ought to facilitate the work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT.
speechtext: We are not paying those clerks yet but shall begin to pay them nest July. That may expedite matters, but in the meantime, the position is that a good deal of the manuscript is not yet in the hands of the printer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT.
speechtext: That is the fault of the departments. If they have not got the work forward, he cannot do it. The Auditor General does not prepare the manuscript

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-'STEAMSHIP COMMUNICATION BETWEEN CANADA AND MEXICO.
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT.
speechtext: Certainly, he prepares the manuscript of his own report. The fault is not with the departments so far as I know. I will see the Auditor General, and perhaps I can give the House more information to-morrow. But I cannot hold out any hope of an early presentation of the Report of the Auditor General.
Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 6 p.m.
Fbiday, January 20, 1905.
